## agent-ml-research
ML research experiment management tools

attachment.content:
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- simplify: Review changed code for reuse, quality, and efficiency, then fix any issues found.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled remote agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring remote agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Build, debug, and optimize Claude API / Anthropic SDK apps. Apps built with this skill should include prompt caching. Also handles migrating existing Claude API code between Claude model versions (4.5 → 4.6, 4.6 → 4.7, retired-model replacements).
TRIGGER when: code imports `anthropic`/`@anthropic-ai/sdk`; user asks for the Claude API, Anthropic SDK, or Managed Agents; user adds/modifies/tunes a Claude feature (caching, thinking, compaction, tool use, batch, files, citations, memory) or model (Opus/Sonnet/Haiku) in a file; questions about prompt caching / cache hit rate in an Anthropic SDK project.
SKIP: file imports `openai`/other-provider SDK, filename like `*-openai.py`/`*-generic.py`, provider-neutral code, general programming/ML.
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- review: Review a pull request
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

87	Near-perfect classification (99.4%) in both conditions. Human text remains trivially separable from all recursive depths even when training data is partially human. This is expected — d0 features are drawn from the original Pythia-1.4B feature space with no LoRA perturbation.

# Accumulation v3 Results Analysis

## 1. Experiment Summary

| Config | mix50 | mix25 |
|--------|-------|-------|
| Model | GPT-2 XL (1.57B) | GPT-2 XL (1.57B) |
| LoRA params | 13.5M (0.86%) | 13.5M (0.86%) |
| Mix ratio | 50% human / 50% synthetic | 25% human / 75% synthetic |
| Training data per depth | 5000 samples | 5000 samples |
| Generated per depth | 5000 samples | 5000 samples |
| Epochs | 3 | 3 |
| Feature extractor | Pythia-1.4B (cross-model) | Pythia-1.4B (cross-model) |
| RF | 200 trees, 5-fold CV | 200 trees, 5-fold CV |
| GPU | CUDA:0 | CUDA:1 |
| Start | 2026-05-19 16:17 CST | 2026-05-19 16:17 CST |
| End | 2026-05-19 20:34 CST | 2026-05-19 20:26 CST |
| Total time | 4.28h (257 min) | 4.14h (248 min) |
| Server | westd-48862 (RTX PRO 6000) | westd-48862 (RTX PRO 6000) |

Pipeline phases (cumulative → per-phase minutes):

| Phase | mix50 | mix25 |
|-------|-------|-------|
| d1 (train+gen) | 104.3 min | 101.6 min |
| d2 (train+gen) | 74.6 min | 71.4 min |
| d3 (train+gen) | 73.8 min | 71.3 min |
| Feature extraction | 3.0 min | 3.0 min |
| RF evaluation | ~1.3 min | ~0.7 min |

Bug fix confirmed: Feature extraction uses Pythia-1.4B (cross-model), not the source GPT-2 XL. This was the bug that invalidated accum_v1/v2.

## 2. Results Comparison

### Main Metrics

| Metric | mix50 | mix25 | Full-replacement | Chance |
|--------|-------|-------|-----------------|--------|
| **4-class accuracy** | 69.1% | **70.1%** | 85.9% | 25.0% |
| **Balanced accuracy** | 69.1% | **70.1%** | 85.9% | 25.0% |
| **d1-d3 balanced acc** | 58.9% | **60.3%** | — | 33.3% |
| Delta vs full-replacement | -16.9 pp | -15.8 pp | — | — |

### Per-Depth Recall

| Depth | mix50 | mix25 | Delta |
|-------|-------|-------|-------|
| d0 (human) | 99.4% | 99.4% | 0.0 |
| d1 | 73.0% | 73.3% | +0.3 |
| d2 | 42.0% | 42.8% | +0.8 |
| d3 | 61.8% | 64.7% | +2.9 |

### Fold Accuracies

| Fold | mix50 | mix25 |
|------|-------|-------|
| 0 | 68.2% | 70.0% |
| 1 | 69.2% | 69.5% |
| 2 | 69.1% | 70.1% |
| 3 | 69.7% | 70.3% |
| 4 | 69.2% | 70.5% |
| Std | 0.5% | 0.4% |

### Confusion Matrices

**mix50:**
```
        pred_d0  pred_d1  pred_d2  pred_d3
true_d0   4968       24        4        4
true_d1     43     3651      904      402
true_d2     27     1168     2102     1703
true_d3     15      512     1383     3090
```

**mix25:**
```
        pred_d0  pred_d1  pred_d2  pred_d3
true_d0   4971       23        6        0
true_d1     35     3667     1006      292
true_d2     21     1247     2142     1590
true_d3     13      391     1360     3236
```

## 3. Per-Depth Analysis

### d0 (Human text)
Near-perfect classification (99.4%) in both conditions. Human text remains trivially separable from all recursive depths even when training data is partially human. This is expected — d0 features are drawn from the original Pythia-1.4B feature space with no LoRA perturbation.

### d1 (First recursive depth)
Stable at ~73% across both mix ratios. d1 misclassifications split toward d2 (18%) and d3 (6-8%). The LoRA fine-tuning at d1 introduces sufficient statistical shift from d0 regardless of human/synthetic proportions.

### d2 (Second recursive depth)
The hardest class at ~42% recall. Heavily confused with both d1 (23-25%) and d3 (32-34%). d2 occupies the "middle ground" in feature space — it has diverged from d1 but hasn't yet reached the d3 attractor. This is the accumulation bottleneck.

### d3 (Third recursive depth)
Shows the largest benefit from lower human mix: 61.8% (mix50) → 64.7% (mix25), a +2.9pp improvement. With more synthetic content in training data, d3 text is pushed further from d2 in feature space, making it more distinguishable.

## 4. Training Loss Trends

| Depth | mix50 loss | mix25 loss | Delta |
|-------|-----------|-----------|-------|
| d1 | 2.131 | 1.918 | -0.213 |
| d2 | 1.892 | 1.586 | -0.306 |
| d3 | 1.789 | 1.434 | -0.355 |

Both conditions show monotonically decreasing loss with depth — each successive depth trains on data that is more synthetic and thus more predictable (lower entropy). mix25 has consistently lower loss because 75% of its training data is synthetic (model-generated), which is inherently easier for the model to fit.

Loss delta widens with depth (0.213 → 0.306 → 0.355), confirming that the compounding effect of more synthetic data in the training mix becomes increasingly pronounced at deeper recursions.

## 5. Key Findings

### Finding 1: Accumulation degrades depth signal by 16-17 pp vs full-replacement
Full-replacement achieves 85.9% 4-class accuracy; accumulation achieves 69-70%. This confirms that full-replacement results are an **upper bound** on feature separability. The ~16pp gap quantifies the cost of realistic accumulation dynamics.

### Finding 2: mix25 slightly outperforms mix50 (counter-intuitive)
Less human data (25%) → slightly better accuracy (70.1% vs 69.1%, +1.0pp). This occurs because:
- With 75% synthetic training data, LoRA adapters learn a stronger "recursive style" at each depth
- d3 text diverges further from human text, making it more classifiable
- The effect is concentrated at d3 (+2.9pp) where the compounding effect is strongest

This is consistent with the model collapse literature: more synthetic contamination → faster statistical divergence → easier detection.

### Finding 3: d2 is the consistent bottleneck
d2 recall (~42%) is well below d1 (~73%) and d3 (~63%). The confusion matrix shows d2 distributing errors nearly evenly between d1 and d3. d2 is in a transitional zone of feature space where accumulation blurs the boundary with adjacent depths.

### Finding 4: Signal is well above chance
Both conditions achieve ~70% accuracy (vs 25% chance), ~60% d1-d3 balanced accuracy (vs 33% chance). Depth signal is degraded but not destroyed by accumulation. The detector can still distinguish recursive depths even with realistic data mixing.

### Finding 5: Invalidated v1/v2 comparison
The invalidated accum_mix50 (feature-space mixing error) reported 35.5% accuracy — far below the correct 69.1%. The invalidated accum_mix25 reported 67.2%, close to the correct 70.1% but for the wrong reasons (feature mixing partially mimicked the statistical effect). The bug fix was essential for scientific validity.

## 6. Implications for Discussion §6 Accumulation Paragraph

### Supports
- **Core claim**: "Full-replacement is an upper bound; accumulation degrades depth signal but does not destroy it." Both mix ratios maintain well-above-chance accuracy.
- **Quantification**: Can now state specific degradation: "Accumulation reduces 4-class accuracy by 16-17 percentage points relative to full-replacement (69-70% vs 86%), while remaining 44-45pp above chance."
- **Monotonic degradation intuition**: Surprisingly, **less human data preserves signal better**, suggesting that the depth detection task benefits from stronger recursive signatures in the training data.

### Modifies
- **Original framing assumed**: more human data → better signal (because closer to full-replacement). The data shows the opposite. The paragraph should note that the relationship between human mix ratio and depth separability is **non-monotonic** or at least **not in the expected direction** at these two data points.
- **Recommended framing**: "Under accumulation, the RF classifier achieves 69-70% 4-class accuracy regardless of whether human text comprises 25% or 50% of the training mix. This stability suggests that depth signal is robust to the specific accumulation ratio within this range, though degraded relative to the full-replacement upper bound (86%). Slightly higher accuracy with 25% human mix (70.1% vs 69.1%) is consistent with the interpretation that stronger recursive contamination at each depth produces more distinctive statistical signatures."

### Additional data needed for complete characterization
- mix0 (0% human / 100% synthetic = full replacement at each depth with LoRA) — would close the curve
- mix75 (75% human / 25% synthetic) — would test whether the trend continues or reverses
- These are low priority; two data points (mix25, mix50) plus full-replacement (effectively mix0) are sufficient for Discussion

## 3. Per-Depth Analysis

### d0 (Human text)
Near-perfect classification (99.4%) in both conditions. Human text remains trivially separable from all recursive depths even when training data is partially human. This is expected — d0 features are drawn from the original Pythia-1.4B feature space with no LoRA perturbation.

### d1 (First recursive depth)
Stable at ~73% across both mix ratios. d1 misclassifications split toward d2 (18%) and d3 (6-8%). The LoRA fine-tuning at d1 introduces sufficient statistical shift from d0 regardless of human/synthetic proportions.

### d2 (Second recursive depth)
The hardest class at ~42% recall. Heavily confused with both d1 (23-25%) and d3 (32-34%). d2 occupies the "middle ground" in feature space — it has diverged from d1 but hasn't yet reached the d3 attractor. This is the accumulation bottleneck.

### d3 (Third recursive depth)
Shows the largest benefit from lower human mix: 61.8% (mix50) → 64.7% (mix25), a +2.9pp improvement. With more synthetic content in training data, d3 text is pushed further from d2 in feature space, making it more distinguishable.

## 5. Key Findings

### Finding 1: Accumulation degrades depth signal by 16-17 pp vs full-replacement
Full-replacement achieves 85.9% 4-class accuracy; accumulation achieves 69-70%. This confirms that full-replacement results are an **upper bound** on feature separability. The ~16pp gap quantifies the cost of realistic accumulation dynamics.

### Finding 2: mix25 slightly outperforms mix50 (counter-intuitive)
Less human data (25%) → slightly better accuracy (70.1% vs 69.1%, +1.0pp). This occurs because:
- With 75% synthetic training data, LoRA adapters learn a stronger "recursive style" at each depth
- d3 text diverges further from human text, making it more classifiable
- The effect is concentrated at d3 (+2.9pp) where the compounding effect is strongest

This is consistent with the model collapse literature: more synthetic contamination → faster statistical divergence → easier detection.

### Finding 3: d2 is the consistent bottleneck
d2 recall (~42%) is well below d1 (~73%) and d3 (~63%). The confusion matrix shows d2 distributing errors nearly evenly between d1 and d3. d2 is in a transitional zone of feature space where accumulation blurs the boundary with adjacent depths.

### Finding 4: Signal is well above chance
Both conditions achieve ~70% accuracy (vs 25% chance), ~60% d1-d3 balanced accuracy (vs 33% chance). Depth signal is degraded but not destroyed by accumulation. The detector can still distinguish recursive depths even with realistic data mixing.

### Finding 5: Invalidated v1/v2 comparison
The invalidated accum_mix50 (feature-space mixing error) reported 35.5% accuracy — far below the correct 69.1%. The invalidated accum_mix25 reported 67.2%, close to the correct 70.1% but for the wrong reasons (feature mixing partially mimicked the statistical effect). - **Core claim**: "Full-replacement is an upper bound; accumulation degrades depth signal but does not destroy it." Both mix ratios maintain well-above-chance accuracy.

- **Monotonic degradation intuition**: Surprisingly, **less human data preserves signal better**, suggesting that the depth detection task benefits from stronger recursive signatures in the training data.

### Modifies
- **Original framing assumed**: more human data → better signal (because closer to full-replacement). The data shows the opposite. The paragraph should note that the relationship between human mix ratio and depth separability is **non-monotonic** or at least **not in the expected direction** at these two data points.

This is a warning-level concern that needs clarification.

Now looking at the GPU situation: both experiments are already done, and the GPUs are idle. Since the project only has these two GPUs available...

Let me check the project constraints and CLAUDE.md to see if there are any gpu_ids restrictions. The constraints.yaml doesn't specify GPU limits, and the project config lists both servers without explicit GPU constraints, so using both GPUs seems fine.

On the "non-monotonic" finding about mix25 outperforming mix50—I should examine whether this is actually counter-intuitive or if there's a reasonable explanation in the data.

Looking at the variance breakdown, the 1.0pp difference between mix ratios is within the cross-seed variance (2.04pp for GPT-2 XL) and fold standard deviation (0.4-0.5%), so this could easily be noise rather than a real signal. The analysis treats it as meaningful and builds causal explanations around it, which is risky for scientific rigor. That said, the recommended framing in the paper is more measured—it acknowledges the slight accuracy difference with 25% human mix but frames it as consistent with the overall pattern rather than a strong finding.

Now I'm compiling my findings to send to the director. The data consistency checks out, the experiment spec is complete, the bug fix is verified, and GPU compliance is fine. But there's a significant issue: the 0.859 baseline for full replacement is hardcoded rather than dynamically computed from an actual run. The hypothesis text references 84.2% from invalidated experiments while the metrics show 85.9%, and neither of the rerun seeds (84.28% and 86.32%) matches that value exactly.

There's also a methodological concern with the mix25 versus mix50 comparison—the 1.0 percentage point difference falls within the seed-level variance I'm seeing across the project, yet the analysis frames it with causal language about model collapse. Since only a single seed was used, I should recommend reporting these as comparable rather than suggesting mix25 is superior.

The core findings hold up though: accumulation clearly degrades performance by around 16-17 percentage points compared to full replacement, the signal stays well above chance at 69-70% versus 25%, class d2 consistently emerges as the bottleneck with ~42% recall, and human text remains trivially separable at ~99.4%. I'm ready to share this with the director.

**结论**: WARNING

### 发现

- [severity: info] **数据一致性通过**：Registry 指标、远程 JSON 结果文件 (`rf_results.json`, `summary.json`)、训练日志三方完全一致。混淆矩阵、fold accuracies、per-class recall 均吻合。

- [severity: info] **实验 spec 完整**：训练命令、服务器(westd-48862)、数据路径+条数(5000/depth)、模型(gpt2-xl LoRA + pythia-1.4b)、seed(42)、checkpoint 路径、log 路径均已记录。

- [severity: info] **GPU 合规**：westd-48862 仅有 2 张 RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell，实验分别占用 cuda:0 和 cuda:1，实验完成后两卡已空闲(0% util, 3MiB)。项目配置未设 gpu_ids 白名单限制，无越界问题。

- [severity: warning] **Full-replacement baseline 0.859 溯源不清**：`accumulation_pipeline_gpt2xl.py` 第 634 行硬编码 `0.859`，不是从对应的 full-replacement 实验动态计算。Registry 中 GPT-2 XL full-replacement 实际数据：seed42 rerun = 84.28%（gpt2xl_seed43_001 记录），seed43 = 86.32%。两者均不等于 85.9%。更严重的是，accum_v3_mix50 的 **hypothesis 文本仍写 "full-replacement (84.2%)"**，但 metrics 用 85.9% 作为 baseline——同一实验内假设与数据不一致。delta 值（-15.8pp / -16.9pp）依赖此 baseline 的正确性。**建议**：明确 0.859 的来源实验 ID，或改为 seed42 rerun 的实际值 0.8428 重新计算 delta。

- [severity: warning] **mix25 vs mix50 差异(+1.0pp)被过度解读**：分析报告 Finding 2 将 1.0pp 差异（70.1% vs 69.1%）定性为 "counter-intuitive"，并构建因果叙事（"consistent with model collapse literature"）。但本项目 GPT-2 XL 跨 seed 方差为 2.04pp（seed42=84.28% vs seed43=86.32%），1.0pp 完全在 seed 噪声范围内。实验仅用单 seed（42），无法区分是真实趋势还是随机波动。**对论文影响**：Discussion §6 应将两个 mix ratio 报告为"comparable"（~69-70%），不宜暗示 mix25 优于 mix50 或构建方向性解释。分析报告 §6.2 的推荐 framing 比 Finding 2 更审慎，但 "non-monotonic" 一词仍不适合——2 个数据点不足以判定单调性。

- [severity: info] **核心结论可信**：accumulation 降低信号 ~16-17pp、信号仍远高于 chance（69-70% vs 25%）、d2 为瓶颈类（~42% recall）、d0 近乎完美分离（99.4%）——这些主结论有充分数据支撑，可用于 Discussion。

### 建议

1. 确认 0.859 baseline 的确切来源（哪个 exp_id / 哪次 run），并在 registry 的 spec 中补充 `baseline_source_exp_id` 字段。如果找不到来源，用 seed42 rerun 值 (0.8428) 重算 delta。
2. 论文 Discussion §6 中避免对 mix25 vs mix50 差异做方向性解读，改为 "both accumulation conditions achieve comparable accuracy (~69–70%)"。
3. 如果需要 claim accumulation ratio 的影响趋势，至少补一个 seed（seed43 对两个 mix ratio）以区分 seed noise 和真实趋势。低优先级——当前两个数据点加 full-replacement 已足够写 Discussion 段落。

file.content:
## 5. Key Findings

### Finding 1: Accumulation degrades depth signal by 16-17 pp vs full-replacement
Full-replacement achieves 85.9% 4-class accuracy; accumulation achieves 69-70%. This confirms that full-replacement results are an **upper bound** on feature separability. The ~16pp gap quantifies the cost of realistic accumulation dynamics.

### Finding 2: mix25 slightly outperforms mix50 (counter-intuitive)
Less human data (25%) → slightly better accuracy (70.1% vs 69.1%, +1.0pp). This occurs because:
- With 75% synthetic training data, LoRA adapters learn a stronger "recursive style" at each depth
- d3 text diverges further from human text, making it more classifiable
- The effect is concentrated at d3 (+2.9pp) where the compounding effect is strongest

This is consistent with the model collapse literature: more synthetic contamination → faster statistical divergence → easier detection.

### Finding 3: d2 is the consistent bottleneck
d2 recall (~42%) is well below d1 (~73%) and d3 (~63%). The confusion matrix shows d2 distributing errors nearly evenly between d1 and d3. d2 is in a transitional zone of feature space where accumulation blurs the boundary with adjacent depths.

### Finding 4: Signal is well above chance
Both conditions achieve ~70% accuracy (vs 25% chance), ~60% d1-d3 balanced accuracy (vs 33% chance). Depth signal is degraded but not destroyed by accumulation. The detector can still distinguish recursive depths even with realistic data mixing.

### Finding 5: Invalidated v1/v2 comparison
The invalidated accum_mix50 (feature-space mixing error) reported 35.5% accuracy — far below the correct 69.1%. The invalidated accum_mix25 reported 67.2%, close to the correct 70.1% but for the wrong reasons (feature mixing partially mimicked the statistical effect). The bug fix was essential for scientific validity.

## 6. Implications for Discussion §6 Accumulation Paragraph

### Supports
- **Core claim**: "Full-replacement is an upper bound; accumulation degrades depth signal but does not destroy it." Both mix ratios maintain well-above-chance accuracy.
- **Quantification**: Can now state specific degradation: "Accumulation reduces 4-class accuracy by 16-17 percentage points relative to full-replacement (69-70% vs 86%), while remaining 44-45pp above chance."
- **Monotonic degradation intuition**: Surprisingly, **less human data preserves signal better**, suggesting that the depth detection task benefits from stronger recursive signatures in the training data.

### Modifies
